summary: Defines how a WebDAV client can use the Prefer header from RFC 7240 to ask the server for particular behavior in building a response. It also defines a new preference called depth-noroot. It updates RFC 7240.

plainLanguage.summary: When ordering at a restaurant, you can say how you would like the meal done. This lets a program ask a file server for how it wants the answer.

questions: what is the prefer header in webdav
what does return=minimal do in webdav
subtitle: How WebDAV clients can use the Prefer header to get smaller responses, fewer round trips, and a way to skip the root resource.

tldr.problem: WebDAV responses can be verbose, and clients often need an extra GET after a change or a failed conditional request. RFC 7240 leaves open what a minimal response should look like.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8144 defines exactly what servers should leave out for return=minimal, recommends return=representation to save round trips (including on 412 responses), and adds a new depth-noroot preference.
tldr.outcome: Clients can ask for leaner answers and fewer round trips. The document updates RFC 7240 and registers the new preference.

today: RFC 8144 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2017 and updates RFC 7240. It has not been obsoleted or updated itself.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
RFC 7240 defines the Prefer header field and the return=minimal preference, but leaves it to the server to decide what a minimal response is. It also defines return=representation, which asks the server to include the resource's current state in the response to a successful request.

RFC 8144 applies these to WebDAV (RFC 4918). Section 2 says precisely what a minimal WebDAV response contains. Section 3 recommends when clients should use return=representation and extends it to 412 (Precondition Failed) responses. Section 4 defines a new preference, depth-noroot. The document updates RFC 7240.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule book from before said you can ask for a short answer but did not say what short means. This one fills in the details.

sections.title: Shorter Answers with return=minimal
sections.content:
Some bodies, such as 207 (Multi-Status) responses, can be quite verbose. For a PROPFIND, or a REPORT whose result is a 207, a request with return=minimal means the server SHOULD omit every DAV:propstat element whose DAV:status is 404 (Not Found). If that would leave a DAV:response with no DAV:propstat, the server MUST substitute either a DAV:propstat with an empty DAV:prop and a 200 (OK) status, or a bare DAV:status of 200 (OK).

For a PROPPATCH where every instruction succeeds, the server SHOULD return 204 (No Content) or 200 (OK), preferably with an empty body, instead of a 207. For MKCALENDAR and extended MKCOL, when the collection is created and all properties are set, the server SHOULD return 201 (Created) with an empty body.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only want to hear about things that worked, the server skips the long list of things that were not found and just says all good when everything worked.

sections.title: Fewer Round Trips with return=representation
sections.content:
After a state-changing request (PUT, COPY/MOVE, PATCH or POST), a client would often issue a GET to see the current state, which may differ from what it sent, for example with CalDAV scheduling. Instead it can add return=representation. On success the server SHOULD include an entity with the current state in the 201 (Created) or 200 (OK) response. That also tells the client the changes came from the server rather than a concurrent client, giving a level of atomicity.

The same applies to conditional requests using If-Match or If-None-Match. If the condition is false, the server SHOULD put the resource's current state in the 412 (Precondition Failed) response, so the client need not fetch it separately.
sections.plainLanguage: When you change a document, the server hands you back the new copy right away, so you do not have to go and ask for it.

sections.title: The depth-noroot Preference
sections.content:
The depth-noroot preference tells the server to leave out the target (root) resource and apply the method only to the resources beneath it. It is meant only for HTTP methods that explicitly support the Depth header, and it applies only when Depth is 1 or infinity, explicitly or implicitly. It MAY be combined with return=minimal in one request.

The appendix explains that this behavior matches the older 1,noroot and infinity,noroot Depth header values, and that the minimal-response behaviors match the Brief header field for PROPFIND and PROPPATCH. If a server gets both Brief and Prefer, clients can expect it to ignore Brief.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking for everything in a folder but not the folder itself, like wanting the toys in the box and not the box.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says no new security considerations come from using Prefer with WebDAV, beyond those in RFC 7240 and those already inherent in the requests.

IANA registered depth-noroot in the HTTP Preferences Registry, and updated the references for the MKCALENDAR, MKCOL, PROPFIND, PROPPATCH and REPORT methods and for status code 412.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking for a shorter answer does not open any new doors for bad guys, and the new option was added to the official list.
